title: Fear Allah, and do not take orders from those against Him.
subtitle: Whose voice gets to steer you
then: Ibn Kathir says when Allah commands His Messenger ﷺ, {idea}the command is even more for those below him{/idea}. Talq bin Habib defined taqwa as obeying Allah by His guidance, hoping for His reward. Do not {trap}listen to or consult{/trap} those working against the message.
now: The group chat that mocks your choices. The voice at work that says everyone bends the rules. {idea}You do not have to take direction from them.{/idea} Allah knows where each path ends.
old: I go with whatever the people around me say.
new: The One who knows every outcome gets the final say in my choices.
try: Before your next big decision, ask yourself whose approval you are really seeking.

title: Follow what your Lord reveals. He sees what you do.
subtitle: The positive side of the command
then: After telling him not to obey those against the message, Allah tells His Messenger ﷺ what to follow instead: {idea}what is revealed, the Qur'an and Sunnah{/idea}. Ibn Kathir says {idea}nothing at all is hidden from Him{/idea}.
now: You unfollow the accounts that drag you down. Good. Then the feed is empty and you fill it with more noise. {idea}Saying no is half.{/idea} The other half is filling that space with what Allah sent.
old: Avoiding bad influences is enough.
new: Turning from the wrong voices only works if I follow the right one.
try: Replace one app or habit you cut back on with ten minutes of Qur'an today.

title: Rely on Allah. He is enough to handle it.
subtitle: Trust after taqwa and following
then: Ibn Kathir says put your trust in Allah {idea}in all your affairs and situations{/idea}. He is {reward}sufficient as a Trustee for the one who trusts Him{/reward} and turns to Him. The surah goes on to describe a siege where this trust was tested.
now: The visa application. The interview. Your child's first night away. You did your part, and still you keep refreshing your email. {reward}Hand the rest to Him.{/reward} He is enough.
old: If I stop worrying, things will fall apart.
new: I do my part, and Allah is enough for the rest.
try: Write down one worry, do one step about it, then say hasbiyallah and put the paper away.

title: No one has two hearts. Words do not change what is real.
subtitle: Saying something does not make it true
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah gives tangible examples: {idea}one man cannot have two hearts{/idea}. Zayd bin Harithah was known as Zayd bin Muhammad, and Allah ended that naming. Ibn Abbas reported the hypocrites claimed the Prophet ﷺ had {trap}two hearts{/trap}, and this verse answered.
now: You label yourself on a bad day: I am useless, I am a failure. You say it so often it feels true. {idea}Saying it does not make it real.{/idea} Allah says the truth, and He guides to the way.
old: If enough people say something, it becomes true.
new: Words from mouths do not change reality. Allah's word does.
try: Catch one label you use about yourself today and replace it with something true.

title: Honour real lineage, and no blame for honest mistakes.
subtitle: Justice in names, mercy in errors
then: Ibn Umar said Zayd was called Zayd bin Muhammad {idea}until this verse came{/idea}. If a father was unknown, Ibn Kathir says they are {reward}brothers in faith{/reward}, to make up for the lost lineage. Mistakes made without intent carry no blame.
now: You mispronounce a new colleague's name for weeks and only find out later. You feel awful. {reward}Allah looks at intention.{/reward} Fix it, and let the guilt go. Then treat every stranger like family.
old: Every mistake I make is counted against me.
new: Allah holds me to what my heart intends, and He forgives.
try: Learn and use the full, correct name of someone you see often.

title: The Prophet ﷺ is closer to believers than they are to themselves.
subtitle: A love and loyalty above self
then: Ibn Kathir says the Prophet ﷺ is {idea}merciful and sincere towards his Ummah{/idea}. He said that if a believer left debts or orphans, {reward}bring them to me and I will take care of them{/reward}. Umar learned to love him more than himself.
now: You do what you feel like, then look for a hadith to back it up. {idea}The verse turns that around.{/idea} The one who cared for orphans and debts he did not owe knows better than your mood.
old: My own feelings should come first in my choices.
new: The Prophet ﷺ cared for me more than I care for myself, so his way comes first.
try: Learn one Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ you do not practise yet, and do it today.

title: A solemn covenant taken from the greatest Messengers.
subtitle: Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Isa, and the Prophet ﷺ
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah took a covenant from the Prophets {idea}to establish His religion, convey the message and support one another{/idea}. The verse names the five of strongest resolve and {reward}begins with the last Prophet ﷺ as a mark of respect{/reward}.
now: You made promises too: at your nikah, when you took the job, when your child was born. {idea}A covenant is heavier than a mood.{/idea} The Prophets kept theirs through rejection and hardship.
old: Promises bend when life gets hard.
new: A serious promise is kept through hardship, as the Prophets kept theirs.
try: Recall one serious promise you made, and do one thing today to honour it.

title: The truthful will be asked about their truth.
subtitle: Why the covenant matters
then: Mujahid said the truthful here are {idea}those who convey the message from the Messengers{/idea}. Ibn Kathir adds: we bear witness that {reward}the Messengers conveyed the message clearly{/reward}, even though some rejected them.
now: Even the most truthful people will be asked. That should make you careful with your own words: the reviews you write, the CV, the reply to your parents. {idea}Truth is something you will be asked about.{/idea}
old: If I am basically honest, no one will question me.
new: Even the truthful are asked, so I want my truth to be complete.
try: Correct one small exaggeration you told recently.

title: Remember the favour: armies came, and He sent a wind.
subtitle: The Battle of the Trench
then: Ibn Kathir says the Confederates, nearly ten thousand, besieged Madinah in 5 AH. On Salman's advice, the Muslims dug a trench, {idea}and the Prophet ﷺ dug and carried earth with them{/idea}. After about a month, Allah sent {reward}an intensely cold wind{/reward} and they left.
now: Bills on one side, a diagnosis on another, a family crisis on top. It feels like everything came at once. {reward}Remember the times He already got you through.{/reward} That is what this verse asks.
old: When everything comes at once, I am on my own.
new: Allah has rescued me before in ways I could not see, and He sees me now.
try: Write down one hard time Allah brought you through, and thank Him for it.

title: Eyes darting, hearts in the throat, thoughts about Allah.
subtitle: What fear does inside you
then: Ibn Kathir says the enemy came from above and below. The eyes grew wild {trap}from intense fear{/trap}. Ibn Jarir said some thought {trap}the outcome would be against the believers{/trap}. Al-Hasan said there were different kinds of thoughts.
now: The hospital corridor, waiting for the doctor. Your heart is in your throat. The quiet thought: maybe Allah has forgotten me. {idea}The verse names that thought honestly.{/idea} Notice it, and choose good thoughts of Him.
old: Good believers never feel this kind of fear.
new: Fear can rise in anyone. What matters is what I then think of Allah.
try: When fear hits today, say: I think well of Allah, and breathe slowly three times.

title: There the believers were tested and shaken hard.
subtitle: A severe shaking, with the Prophet ﷺ among them

row.title: tests sort hearts
sub: the Prophet ﷺ was right there

then: Ibn Kathir says the Muslims were besieged in {trap}straitened circumstances, with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in their midst{/trap}. They were tried and shaken. {idea}At this time, hypocrisy came out{/idea}, and the weak in faith spoke what was in their hearts.
now: The redundancy round at work. Everyone's real character shows in a week. {idea}Hard seasons reveal what was already inside.{/idea} Being shaken is not a sign Allah has left you. Even the Companions were shaken.
old: If I am being shaken, I must be doing something wrong.
new: Even the best believers were shaken. A shaking shows what is in the heart.
try: In a hard moment today, notice what your first words are, and make them good.

title: Under pressure, some said the promise was a delusion.
subtitle: When hardship brings out hidden doubt
then: Ibn Kathir says {trap}their hypocrisy became apparent{/trap}, and the one with doubt grew weak and voiced it. Ibn Ishaq reported one said they were promised the treasures of Chosroes and Caesar, yet {trap}could not safely go out to relieve themselves{/trap}.
now: You prayed for the job and got rejected. The first thought: maybe none of this works. {idea}Pressure brings out what is underneath.{/idea} Watch what you say when things go wrong, and strengthen it before the next test.
old: When dua is not answered fast, maybe it does not work.
new: Pressure shows me where my faith is thin, so I can strengthen it.
try: Next time something goes wrong, say alhamdulillah before any complaint.

title: Our houses are exposed, they said. They only wanted to flee.
subtitle: An excuse that hid the real reason
then: During the siege, some told the people of Madinah to go home. Ibn Abbas said a group asked permission, saying {trap}we fear our homes may be robbed{/trap}. Allah said their homes were not exposed. {trap}They only wanted to run{/trap} from where they were needed.
now: The volunteer rota at the masjid, the family member who needs a carer this weekend. Suddenly you have a work thing. {idea}Allah knows the real reason{/idea} behind the excuse, even when you half-believe it yourself.
old: My excuse is valid, so I am off the hook.
new: Allah sees whether my reason is real or just a way to escape.
try: Next time you reach for an excuse, ask yourself honestly what the real reason is.

title: Faith that would fold at the first real pressure.
subtitle: How shallow commitment behaves
then: Ibn Kathir, citing Qatadah and Ibn Jarir, says if the enemy had entered and demanded disbelief, {trap}they would have given in promptly{/trap}. They would not stay firm {trap}if faced with the slightest fear{/trap}.
now: The new job where drinks after work are expected. The friends who laugh when you step out to pray. {idea}Pressure is quiet, not dramatic.{/idea} Faith with roots is built before the test arrives.
old: I will be strong when a real test comes.
new: Firmness is built in small daily choices, before the big test.
try: Practise one small act of faith in public today that you usually hide.

title: They had promised Allah. A promise to Him is asked about.
subtitle: Covenants made in calm times
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah reminds them of {idea}the promise they made before the fear struck{/idea}: that they would not turn their backs. {trap}Allah will inevitably ask them about that covenant.{/trap}
now: Ramadan, when you promised yourself you would keep praying Fajr. The hospital visit when you swore you would call your father more. {idea}Those were promises to Allah too.{/idea} He will ask about them.
old: Promises I made in emotional moments do not really count.
new: A promise to Allah is remembered and asked about, even if I forget it.
try: Pick one promise to Allah from a past Ramadan and restart it today, small.

title: Running from death does not buy you more time.
subtitle: Fleeing changes nothing about your appointed term
then: Ibn Kathir says fleeing {idea}will not delay their appointed end or lengthen their lives{/idea}. It may even bring it sooner. He links it to 4:77: {reward}the enjoyment of this world is short, the Hereafter is better{/reward}.
now: You avoid the hard conversation, the hospital visit, the responsibility, as if dodging them keeps you safe. {idea}Your time is already written.{/idea} What you do with it is the part you choose.
old: If I avoid every hard thing, I will be safer.
new: My time is set by Allah, so running from duty buys me nothing.
try: Do one thing today you have been avoiding out of fear.

title: Who can shield you from Allah, if He wills harm or mercy?
subtitle: No protector or helper but Him
then: Ibn Kathir says {idea}they have no one except Allah to respond to their cries{/idea}. Those fleeing the trench imagined safety elsewhere. But no one can block what He wills, {reward}whether harm or mercy{/reward}.
now: The mercy you are waiting for: a job, a child, healing. No one can stop it if He wills it. {reward}And no one can give it if He does not.{/reward} So the only place to run is to Him.
old: If I find the right person, they can protect me from anything.
new: Only Allah can block harm or send mercy, so I run to Him.
try: Ask Allah directly today for one mercy you have been waiting for.

title: Allah knows who holds others back from doing good.
subtitle: The ones who say come here, stay comfortable
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah's knowledge covers those who {trap}told others not to go out{/trap}, saying to friends: come to us, to {trap}the shade and the fruits{/trap}. They themselves came to the battle only a little.
now: Your friend is about to start memorising Qur'an, or volunteer on weekends. You say: relax, you do too much. {idea}Notice when you are the voice holding someone back.{/idea}
old: Talking someone out of a hard good deed is just being caring.
new: Allah knows when I hold others back from good, even gently.
try: Encourage one person today in a good thing they are trying to do.

title: Frozen in fear, then sharp-tongued once it is safe.
subtitle: Cowardice in danger, boasting after
then: Ibn Kathir says when security returned, they spoke eloquently, {trap}claiming they were the bravest{/trap}. Qatadah said at sharing time they were the loudest: {trap}give us, we were there with you{/trap}. In battle they had been the most absent.
now: The group project where one person vanished, then presented the slides. The family crisis where someone showed up only for the will reading. {idea}Check whether you are ever that person.{/idea}
old: I can take credit as long as I was around.
new: Quiet presence in hard times matters more than loud claims later.
try: Give credit today to someone who did work that you might be praised for.

title: They wished to be far away, asking for news from a distance.
subtitle: Watching from the sidelines
then: Ibn Kathir says even after the Confederates left, they thought {trap}the armies were still nearby{/trap}. If they came back, these men would rather be {trap}out in the desert asking for news{/trap} than with the believers in Madinah.
now: A relative is sick and you follow it on the family group chat, never visiting. A friend is struggling and you just watch their stories. {idea}Asking for news from far away is not the same as being there.{/idea}
old: Keeping updated from a distance is enough support.
new: Being present when it is hard is what loyalty means.
try: Visit or call someone going through a hard time, instead of just checking updates.

title: In the Messenger of Allah ﷺ you have the best example.
subtitle: For whoever hopes in Allah and remembers Him much
then: Ibn Kathir calls this {idea}an important principle: follow the Messenger ﷺ in his words and deeds{/idea}. At Al-Ahzab, people were told to copy his {reward}patience, guarding, striving and waiting for Allah's way out{/reward}. It was said to those who panicked.
now: Crisis at work, panic in the family chat, everyone shouting. You ask: what would he ﷺ do here? {idea}Patient, present, working, trusting.{/idea} That question changes how you walk into the room.
old: The Prophet's ﷺ example is for worship, not for crises at work.
new: His example covers how I act under pressure, every day.
try: In your next stressful moment, pause and ask how the Prophet ﷺ would respond.

title: Seeing the armies, the believers said: this is what was promised.
subtitle: Hardship that increased faith
then: Ibn Abbas and Qatadah said the believers remembered 2:214: {idea}trials come, then the help of Allah is near{/idea}. So seeing the armies {reward}only added to their faith{/reward}. Ibn Kathir notes that faith can increase and decrease.
now: The same layoff email reaches two colleagues. One says Allah has abandoned me. The other says I was told life would test me, and help is near. {reward}Same email, different heart.{/reward}
old: Hardship means my faith is failing.
new: Hardship can be the very thing that grows my faith, if I read it right.
try: When something hard happens today, say: this is what Allah and His Messenger promised.

title: Men who were true to their promise, and never changed.
subtitle: Some fulfilled it, some are still waiting
then: Anas bin Malik said his uncle Anas bin An-Nadr missed Badr and said: {idea}if Allah shows me another battle, Allah will see what I do{/idea}. At Uhud he said he found {reward}the fragrance of Paradise{/reward} and was martyred. They thought this verse was about him.
now: You do not need a battlefield. You made a quiet vow: to look after your parents, to stay honest at work, to keep your prayers. {idea}Some are still waiting to fulfil it.{/idea} The test is to never change it.
old: Big promises are only for heroic people in history.
new: Staying true to my quiet promise to Allah, without changing, is the same path.
try: Say to yourself one promise you made to Allah, and renew it today without telling anyone.

title: The truthful are rewarded, and the door stays open for others.
subtitle: Justice for the true, mercy offered to the false
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah tests with fear and shaking {idea}to tell the evil from the good{/idea}, by their deeds. Even for hypocrites, He may {reward}guide them to give up hypocrisy{/reward}, because His mercy prevails over His wrath.
now: You have been two-faced: one person at the masjid, another at the party. You feel like the verse is about you. {reward}It ends on Forgiving, Merciful.{/reward} The door is open. Walk through it.
old: I have been fake for too long to be forgiven.
new: Allah's mercy prevails, and the door to change is open for me.
try: Choose one area where you act differently in different crowds, and make it consistent today.

title: Allah sent them back enraged and spared the believers a fight.
subtitle: He alone defeated the Confederates
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah {reward}sufficed for the believers{/reward}, so they did not have to fight. The Prophet ﷺ used to say: {idea}He was true to His promise, helped His servant, and defeated the Confederates alone{/idea}.
now: You prepared for weeks for the hearing, the confrontation, the meeting you dreaded. Then it just dissolved. {reward}You did not have to fight.{/reward} Do not credit your planning. Thank Him.
old: When things work out, it is because I prepared well.
new: I prepare, but Allah is the one who settles it, sometimes before I lift a finger.
try: Say the Prophet's ﷺ words today: la ilaha illallahu wahdah, sadaqa wa'dah.

title: Breaking a sworn agreement in a moment of crisis.
subtitle: The weight of betraying a covenant
then: Ibn Kathir says Banu Qurayzah had {idea}a treaty with the Prophet ﷺ and were under his protection{/idea}. During the siege, they were persuaded to {trap}break the covenant{/trap}, which deeply distressed the believers. After the Confederates left, the verse tells how they were brought down from their forts.
now: A colleague trusted you with a confidence. Then the office politics shift and sharing it could help you. {trap}The temptation to switch sides is real.{/trap} {idea}Keeping your word when it costs you{/idea} is the lesson here.
old: Agreements can be dropped when circumstances change.
new: A promise is tested most when breaking it looks profitable.
try: Keep one confidence or commitment today that would be easier to break.

title: Lands, homes, and wealth given, and land not yet walked.
subtitle: Allah is able to do all things

row.title: Allah, able over all
sub: even where I have not walked

then: Days earlier, the believers were besieged and {trap}hearts reached their throats{/trap}. Now this verse says Allah {reward}gave them land, homes and wealth{/reward}, and promised {idea}a land they had not yet set foot on{/idea}. Allah is able to do all things.
now: Last year you could not see a way out: the debt, the job hunt, the waiting. Now look where you are. {idea}There is ground ahead you have not walked yet.{/idea} The One who turned it around is still able.
old: I can only hope for what I can already see.
new: Allah can open doors I have not even walked toward yet.
try: Write down one thing you have now that you once only prayed for, and thank Allah.

title: If you want the world and its glitter, you may go.
subtitle: The Prophet's ﷺ wives were given a choice
then: Jabir reported the wives were asking the Prophet ﷺ for spending he did not have. Allah told him to offer them a choice. He began with Aisha and said {idea}do not hurry, consult your parents first{/idea}. He said Allah {idea}sent him to teach gently{/idea}.
now: The argument at home about money: the holiday, the new car, what the neighbours have. {idea}He did not shout or pressure.{/idea} He laid out the choice calmly and gave time. That is a way to have hard talks.
old: Hard conversations at home need to be settled fast and firmly.
new: A hard choice can be offered gently, with time to think.
try: In your next tense money talk at home, lower your voice and offer time to think.

title: They chose Allah, His Messenger, and the Home of the Hereafter.
subtitle: A great reward for those who choose well
then: Aisha said: {reward}do I need to consult my parents about you? I choose Allah and His Messenger{/reward}. All the wives did the same, choosing {idea}to patiently bear the straitened life with him{/idea}. Ibn Kathir says Allah then gave them the best of both worlds.
now: A better-paid job that would mean dropping your prayers and your family time. A shiny offer with a hidden cost. {reward}Some choices are clear once you name what is on each side.{/reward}
old: Choosing the Hereafter means losing out in this life.
new: Choosing Allah first is never a loss. He gives the best of both.
try: Name one current choice, and write what is on the world's side and what is on Allah's side.

title: Higher status, heavier responsibility.
subtitle: Why the stakes were doubled for the Prophet's ﷺ wives
then: Ibn Kathir says this is {idea}a conditional phrase, and does not imply it actually happened{/idea}. Because their status was so high, a sin would be worse, and this protects them. The next verse doubles {reward}their reward for obedience{/reward}.
now: You are the imam's son, the teacher, the one everyone asks for advice. {idea}Your slip carries further than others.{/idea} So does your good example. Position is not privilege. It is weight.
old: Being respected gives me a bit more room for mistakes.
new: The more people look to me, the more carefully I should walk.
try: Think of one person who looks up to you, and do one thing today worth copying.

title: Higher place, double weight, and double reward.
subtitle: Why a closer seat raises both stakes

picture.label: The wives of the Prophet ﷺ

then: The verse before warned the wives of the Prophet ﷺ that a wrong from them would weigh double. Ibn Kathir notes this is a conditional, not a claim it happened. This verse is the other side: {reward}obedience and good deeds from them earn reward twice over{/reward}, with a noble provision in Paradise.
now: You are the eldest sibling, the team lead, the one people watch at the masjid. When you slip, it echoes. When you hold steady, others hold steady too. {idea}A visible place multiplies what you do{/idea}, the good as much as the bad.
old: Being looked up to just means more pressure on me.
new: A closer place means my good deeds carry further too, and Allah rewards that.
try: Think of one person who watches how you act. Do one good thing today with them in mind.

title: Speak clearly and decently, leave no opening for a sick heart.
subtitle: The tone of a voice can open doors
then: Allah tells the wives of the Prophet ﷺ that they are not like other women, and their manners would be an example for the women of the Ummah. Ibn Zayd explained honorable speech as decent talk known to be good. {trap}A soft, coaxing tone can feed a heart that is already sick.{/trap}
now: The late-night messages with a coworker that drift from work to something warmer. The jokes in DMs that slowly change tone. Nothing said was wrong on paper. {idea}Clear, kind, decent speech keeps the door where it should be.{/idea}
old: If my words are polite, how I say them does not matter.
new: How I speak sends a message too, so I keep my tone honest and clean.
try: Reread your last few chats with someone outside your family. Keep the next one clear and decent.

title: Allah wants to lift the dirt off you and purify you.
subtitle: Commands as a cleaning, not a cage

row.title: a wish to purify
sub: Allah wants to remove the dirt

then: The wives of the Prophet ﷺ are told to stay in their homes except for a need, to avoid the showy display of the days of ignorance, to pray, give zakah, and obey. Ibn Kathir says Allah {trap}first forbids the harmful{/trap}, then {idea}commands the good{/idea}. The aim is stated plainly: to purify the Prophet's household ﷺ.
now: You scroll past a hundred people performing their lives for strangers. You feel the pull to do the same. Then the prayer time alert pops up. {idea}One pulls you outward to be seen, the other pulls you inward to be cleaned.{/idea}
old: Rules about how I carry myself are just limits on my freedom.
new: Behind the command is a wish to clean me, not to box me in.
try: Before posting anything today, ask: is this for being seen, or for something good? Then decide.

title: Remember what is recited in your homes.
subtitle: A house where revelation is heard
then: The wives of the Prophet ﷺ lived where revelation came down and where his words of wisdom were spoken. They are told to {idea}remember what was recited in their homes{/idea}. The verse ends with Allah being Subtle and Well-Acquainted, aware of every quiet detail.
now: Your home has a sound. The TV in the background, the news on the radio, the phone videos on speaker at dinner. {idea}What is recited in a house shapes the people in it.{/idea} A few verses at Fajr change that sound.
old: My home is just where I rest between the important things.
new: What is heard in my home is part of my worship and my family's shaping.
try: Recite or play a short surah aloud at home today where others can hear it.

title: Ten qualities, named for men and women alike.
subtitle: Umm Salamah asked, and the answer came
then: Umm Salamah asked the Prophet ﷺ why women were not mentioned in the Quran as men were. One day she heard him from the minbar reciting this verse. {reward}Every quality is named twice: for men and for women.{/reward} Each one is a step of faith, ending with those who remember Allah much.
now: You sit in a talk where it feels like the message is for someone else. Too young, too old, wrong gender, wrong background. This verse lists ten qualities and puts {idea}your name beside each one{/idea}. The door is the same for everyone.
old: The big promises are for other kinds of people, not someone like me.
new: Allah named each quality for men and women alike. The reward is open to me.
try: Pick one of the ten qualities in this verse that you want more of. Practice it once today.

title: When Allah has decided, the believer does not shop around.
subtitle: A young woman who trusted the Prophet's choice ﷺ

row.title: I will see if it suits me

then: The Prophet ﷺ proposed a marriage for Julaybib, a man the family did not expect. Her parents hesitated, but the young woman said: {idea}are you refusing the command of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ? I will not come to harm.{/idea} Julaybib was later martyred, and {reward}the Prophet ﷺ prayed that blessings be poured on her{/reward}.
now: You know what is right in a matter. Then you start collecting opinions, looking for the one that lets you off. A friend, a forum, a search result. {trap}Shopping for permission{/trap} feels like thinking, but it is often just delay.
old: Even after Allah has spoken, I still get to decide if it suits me.
new: When Allah and His Messenger ﷺ have decided, trusting it is the safer path.
try: Name one clear thing you keep putting off. Take the first step on it today, without asking around.

title: Allah has more right to be feared than people.
subtitle: Breaking a custom that only looked sacred
then: Zayd bin Harithah, freed and once called the son of Muhammad ﷺ, had a difficult marriage with Zaynab bint Jahsh. The Prophet ﷺ told him to keep his wife and fear Allah. Allah then married Zaynab to the Prophet ﷺ, so that {idea}believers would no longer feel blocked by the custom about adopted sons' former wives{/idea}. 'A'ishah said if he had hidden any verse, it would have been this one.
now: Your family has a habit everyone treats as religion, but it is only custom. You know it, and you know saying so will cause talk at the next gathering. {trap}The fear of the group chat is real.{/trap} {idea}Allah has more right to be feared.{/idea}
old: Some things I stay quiet about because of what people would say.
new: If Allah has made it clear, people's talk does not get the final word.
try: Notice one choice today you are making only to avoid people's comments. Ask what Allah wants instead.

title: No blame in what Allah has made his duty.
subtitle: The same way Allah treated earlier prophets
then: Ibn Kathir says this answers {trap}the hypocrites who imagined something wrong{/trap} in the Prophet's marriage to Zaynab ﷺ. Allah never commanded earlier prophets to do anything blameworthy. {idea}His command, once decreed, comes to pass.{/idea}
now: You make a choice that is fully halal, and the comments start. A relative frowns, a colleague asks a pointed question. You start to feel guilty for something that has no sin in it. {idea}Their discomfort is not Allah's verdict.{/idea}
old: If people around me disapprove, I must be doing something wrong.
new: When Allah has allowed it, others' disapproval does not make it a fault.
try: If you carry guilt over a choice that is not a sin, say so to yourself and let it go.

title: They fear Allah and no one else, so they keep delivering.
subtitle: The messengers who were not stopped by threats
then: Allah praises those who convey His message, fear Him, and fear no one else. Ibn Kathir says {idea}no threat could stop them{/idea}, and the leader in this was the Prophet ﷺ, sent to all people. Then {reward}his Companions and each generation after inherited the task{/reward}.
now: Someone at work says something cruel about a colleague who is not there. Everyone laughs. You know a gentle word would help, but your throat goes tight. {idea}Fearing only Allah makes that one sentence possible.{/idea}
old: I will speak up when it is safe and nobody minds.
new: If I fear Allah most, other people's reaction shrinks to its real size.
try: Say one true, kind thing today that you would usually swallow out of fear.

title: Not anyone's father, but the last brick of prophethood.
subtitle: The Seal of the Prophets ﷺ
then: After this verse it was no longer allowed to say Zayd bin Muhammad. Ibn Kathir notes that none of the Prophet's sons ﷺ lived to adulthood. The Prophet ﷺ described himself as {idea}the one brick that completed a beautiful house built by the prophets before him{/idea}.
now: New voices appear every week claiming a fresh revelation, a new teacher who has the final word. Your feed is full of them. {idea}The house is already complete.{/idea} What you need is to live in it, not wait for another brick.
old: Maybe I need some new message to finally tell me how to live.
new: The guidance is complete. My work is to follow what has already come.
try: Read one authentic saying of the Prophet ﷺ today and act on it once.

title: The one duty with no upper limit: remembering Allah.
subtitle: Keep your tongue moist with His name
then: A man told the Prophet ﷺ that the laws of Islam felt like too much, and asked for one thing to hold on to. He ﷺ said: {idea}keep your tongue moist with the remembrance of Allah.{/idea} Ibn 'Abbas said every duty has a known limit except dhikr, which fits {reward}night and day, sick or well, travelling or home{/reward}.
now: Waiting for the kettle. Stuck at a red light. Lying awake at 2am. Those small dead minutes add up to hours. {idea}Each one can hold a quiet SubhanAllah.{/idea} No mat, no wudu, no special time required.
old: I do my prayers. Remembering Allah beyond that is for very pious people.
new: Dhikr has no limit and needs no setup. Any moment of my day can hold it.
try: Pick one daily wait, like the kettle or traffic, and make it your dhikr moment today.

title: Glorify Him at both ends of the day.
subtitle: Morning and evening as bookends
then: Right after the call to remember Allah much, this verse names two times: morning and late afternoon. Ibn Kathir links it to the verse about glorifying Allah {idea}when evening comes and when morning comes{/idea}. Scholars later wrote whole books of adhkar for these times.
now: Your first touch of the day is the phone: emails, notifications, news. Your last is the same. {trap}The screen owns both ends of your day.{/trap} {idea}Two minutes of glorifying Allah at each end changes what frames everything else.{/idea}
old: Mornings are for rushing and evenings are for collapsing.
new: Starting and ending with Allah's praise gives the whole day a frame.
try: Tomorrow, say SubhanAllah wa bihamdih a few times before you unlock your phone.

title: You remember Him, and He praises you to the angels.
subtitle: Out of darkness into light

row.title: He brings me out
sub: with mercy and the angels' prayers

then: Ibn Kathir explains Allah's salah as {reward}His praise of His servant before the angels{/reward}, or His mercy, and the angels' salah as their prayers for forgiveness. Through this He brings believers out of the darkness of ignorance into light. The Prophet ﷺ once said, of a mother clutching her child, that {idea}Allah will not throw His beloved into the Fire{/idea}.
now: A hard week. You feel invisible, like nobody notices if you try. You say a quiet prayer on the bus home. {reward}Somewhere beyond what you can see, your name is mentioned with praise.{/reward} The pull out of the dark is not yours alone.
old: Getting out of this dark place is all on me.
new: When I turn to Him, Allah and His angels are working to bring me into light.
try: When you feel low today, say one line of dhikr and remember that He mentions you too.

title: The first word when you meet Him: Peace.
subtitle: How the believers will be greeted
then: This verse closes the passage on remembering Allah. Those who remembered Him much will be greeted on the Day they meet Him with {reward}Salam, peace{/reward}. A generous reward is already waiting for them.
now: You walk into a family home after years away, nervous about how they will greet you. Then someone smiles and says, welcome. Everything relaxes. {idea}The believers' meeting with Allah begins with peace.{/idea}
old: Thinking about meeting Allah only makes me anxious.
new: For those who remembered Him, the meeting begins with a greeting of peace.
try: Give someone a warm, full salam today and think of the greeting you hope to hear.

title: Witness, bringer of good news, and warner.
subtitle: Three roles of the Prophet ﷺ
then: 'Abdullah bin 'Amr said the Prophet ﷺ was described in the Tawrah with these same words, and also that {idea}he was not harsh, nor loud in the markets, and he forgave rather than repaying evil{/idea}. He is a witness to Allah's Oneness and over people's deeds, bringing good news and warning.
now: When you remind a friend about something, you tend to go one way. Either all fear, or all reassurance. {idea}The Prophet ﷺ held both, and gently.{/idea} Not loud, not harsh, and quick to forgive.
old: To help someone change, I need to either scare them or comfort them.
new: Real guidance carries good news and warning together, with gentleness.
try: Next time you advise someone, start with one piece of good news before any warning.

title: A caller to Allah and a lamp that spreads light.
subtitle: Light that shows the way without burning

row.title: light up the path
sub: those who want to see, see

then: The Prophet ﷺ calls people to their Lord because Allah commanded it, not on his own account. Ibn Kathir says the message he brought is {idea}as clear as the sun shining brightly{/idea}, and only the stubborn deny it. A lamp in the dark does not argue. It shines.
now: You want your brother to come back to prayer. You have tried lectures, guilt, forwarded videos. {trap}Pushing harder made him pull away.{/trap} {idea}A lamp works by shining: your calm, your honesty, your kindness at home.{/idea}
old: To bring someone to the truth, I have to win the argument.
new: My job is to invite and to shine. The seeing belongs to Allah.
try: Instead of advising someone today, show the good you want for them through one kind act.

title: Give the believers good news of a great bounty.
subtitle: Hope is part of the message
then: Among the Prophet's tasks ﷺ in this passage is a happy one: {reward}tell the believers that a great bounty awaits them from Allah{/reward}. Ibn Kathir describes him as a bearer of glad tidings to the believers of a great reward. Good news is part of the message, not a side note.
now: Every reminder you hear online seems to be about what you are doing wrong. You start to feel your faith as a long list of failures. {reward}This verse is a command to give believers good news.{/reward} You are allowed to feel hopeful.
old: Feeling hopeful about my faith seems almost arrogant.
new: Allah told His Prophet ﷺ to bring believers good news. Hope is part of faith.
try: Share one hopeful verse or saying with a friend who seems discouraged today.

title: Do not follow them, do not hurt them, rely on Allah.
subtitle: Ignoring harm without returning it
then: The Prophet ﷺ faced pressure from disbelievers and hypocrites in Madinah. Ibn Kathir explains: {idea}do not obey them or pay attention to what they say{/idea}, and overlook their harm, because {reward}their matter rests with Allah, and He is enough{/reward}.
now: Someone posts something nasty about you. You have two urges: change yourself to please them, or reply with something sharper. {idea}There is a third path: do not follow them, do not hurt them, and hand it to Allah.{/idea}
old: If someone attacks me, I either give in or strike back.
new: I can refuse their pressure and still not return their harm. Allah is enough.
try: Next time someone provokes you today, do not reply. Say hasbiyallah and move on.

title: Even when it ends early, end it with grace.
subtitle: A gift and a beautiful release
then: This verse speaks of a marriage contract that ends before the couple lived together. Ibn Kathir says it contains several rulings for scholars. Its heart is the instruction: {reward}give her a gift and let her go in a beautiful way{/reward}. Even a short bond deserves a dignified ending.
now: A deal falls through, an engagement is called off, a job offer is withdrawn. It is tempting to just go silent and disappear. {trap}Ghosting feels easier.{/trap} {idea}The verse asks for a gift and a kind goodbye.{/idea}
old: If something ends early, I owe the other person nothing.
new: How I end things matters to Allah. Even a short bond deserves a kind ending.
try: Think of a connection you ended badly. Send one kind, respectful message if it is wise to.

title: Allah set the Prophet's limits so he would feel no hardship.
subtitle: Special rules for a special role ﷺ

picture.label: What Allah explained to him ﷺ

then: Allah tells the Prophet ﷺ which marriages are lawful for him, including some {idea}given only to him and not to other believers{/idea}. Ibn Kathir calls the permission for cousins a balanced middle path. The verse says the aim was that there be {reward}no difficulty on him{/reward}, and ends with Allah's forgiveness and mercy.
now: You compare your life to someone else's and wonder why their rules seem different. A doctor on call, a parent of a sick child, a person with a heavy role. {idea}Allah knows what each role needs.{/idea} His limits are set with care, not at random.
old: If someone has different allowances than me, it must be unfair.
new: Allah sets each limit with knowledge, to remove hardship, not to add it.
try: Notice one time today you judge someone's situation by your own. Pause and leave it to Allah.

title: Allah knows what is in your hearts, and He is Forbearing.
subtitle: Fair in actions, honest about feelings
then: Allah gave the Prophet ﷺ choice in how he arranged his time with his wives. Yet 'A'ishah said he divided it fairly and prayed: {idea}O Allah, this is what I do in what I control, so do not blame me for what You control and I do not{/idea}, meaning matters of the heart. The verse closes with {reward}Allah All-Knowing and Forbearing{/reward}.
now: You are a parent who feels closer to one child. A teacher who clicks with one student. You feel guilty for something you cannot switch off. {idea}Make your actions fair, and leave the heart's leanings with Allah.{/idea}
old: If I feel more for one person, I have already been unjust.
new: Allah knows my heart. I am asked to be fair in what I can control.
try: Pick one person you may be neglecting compared to another. Give them some time today.

title: They chose him, and Allah honored that choice.
subtitle: A limit given as a reward for loyalty

picture.label: A reward in the form of a limit

then: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and others said this verse was {reward}a reward for the Prophet's wives ﷺ{/reward} after they chose Allah, His Messenger, and the Hereafter. Allah restricted him to them. 'A'ishah later said the restriction was lifted, but {idea}he married no one else{/idea}, making his loyalty to them clear.
now: You stayed with your family business through the hard years when others left. You stood by a friend when it was not popular. Nobody thanked you. {reward}Allah sees the choice and honors it{/reward}, sometimes in ways you only notice later.
old: Staying loyal when it costs me is something nobody will ever notice.
new: Allah watches over all things, and He honors those who choose Him.
try: Thank someone who stayed loyal to you through a hard time. Tell them specifically.

title: The Prophet ﷺ was too shy to ask, so Allah said it.
subtitle: Guests who stayed too long

row.title: the Prophet ﷺ
sub: too shy to ask them to go

then: Anas said that after the Prophet's wedding feast ﷺ for Zaynab, {trap}three men stayed on, talking in the house{/trap}. He ﷺ was extremely shy and kept leaving and returning rather than asking them to go. Then this verse came: come when invited, leave after the meal, for {idea}Allah is not shy of the truth{/idea}.
now: You are at a friend's place. The baby is crying, the host keeps glancing at the clock, and you are still on your third story. They will never say it. {idea}Good manners means noticing what people are too polite to say.{/idea}
old: If my host has not asked me to leave, I am welcome to stay.
new: Caring for others means reading what they are too shy to say.
try: Next time you visit someone, leave a little earlier than you feel like leaving.

title: Shown or hidden, Allah already knows.
subtitle: The quiet line after the rules
then: After the verse on entering the Prophet's homes ﷺ and the manners of speaking with his wives, this short verse follows. {idea}Whether you reveal something or conceal it, Allah knows it all.{/idea} The rules were about behavior, and this line reaches the heart behind it.
now: You are polite to your manager face to face, then type something sour about them in a private chat. Nobody at work will see it. {idea}The closed chat is not closed to Allah.{/idea}
old: What I keep private does not really count.
new: Allah knows what I hide as well as what I show. Both shape who I am.
try: Delete or stop one private habit today that you would hide from people you respect.

title: With close family there is ease, and Allah still watches.
subtitle: The circle where the screen is lifted
then: After the command of the screen, Allah names the close relatives before whom the wives of the Prophet ﷺ were free of it. Ibn Kathir links it to the similar list in Surat An-Nur. The verse ends with {idea}have taqwa of Allah, for He witnesses everything{/idea}, in private as in public.
now: At home you finally relax. Shoes off, guard down. That is a mercy. But home is also where you snap at your mother or scroll what you would never scroll in public. {idea}Ease at home and awareness of Allah can live together.{/idea}
old: At home with family I can let go of everything.
new: Home is a place of ease, and Allah is still Witness there.
try: Be as gentle with your family tonight as you would be with a guest.

title: Allah and His angels send blessings on him, so join in.
subtitle: Sending salah and salam on the Prophet ﷺ
then: The Companions asked the Prophet ﷺ how to send salah on him, and he taught them the words: {idea}O Allah, send Your salah on Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You did on the family of Ibrahim{/idea}. He once heard a man make dua without praising Allah or sending salah, and said {trap}this man is rushing{/trap}.
now: You need something badly: a test result, a visa, a reply. You raise your hands and jump straight to the request. {idea}Start with praise, then salah on the Prophet ﷺ, then ask.{/idea} You join something Allah and the angels are already doing.
old: When I make dua, I just get straight to what I need.
new: Praising Allah and sending salah on the Prophet ﷺ first is how dua is taught.
try: In your next dua, praise Allah, send salah on the Prophet ﷺ, then ask.

title: Hurting the Messenger ﷺ is hurting what Allah honors.
subtitle: The weight of insulting what is sacred
then: Ibn Kathir says this warns those who persist in defying Allah and who {trap}accuse His Messenger ﷺ of faults{/trap}. He cites a hadith where Allah says the son of Adam annoys Him by cursing time, though {idea}Allah is the One who turns night and day{/idea}. Whoever harms the Prophet ﷺ harms what Allah honors.
now: A bad week and you mutter, this year is cursed, life is against me. It sounds harmless. {idea}Behind the days is Allah.{/idea} Cursing the days quietly aims at the One who turns them.
old: Complaining about fate or bad luck is just letting off steam.
new: Allah runs the days. I can be honest about pain without cursing what He decrees.
try: Next time you want to curse your luck, say instead: Allah, make this easy for me.

title: Saying what they never did is slander and plain sin.
subtitle: Harming believers with false stories
then: Ibn Kathir explains this as attributing to believing men and women {trap}things they did not do, to shame them{/trap}. The Prophet ﷺ was asked about backbiting: mentioning your brother with what he dislikes. And if it is true? {idea}If it is true, you backbit him. If not, you slandered him.{/idea}
now: The family group chat lights up with a story about a cousin's divorce. Nobody checked it. Everybody forwards it. {trap}You carry what you pass on.{/trap} {idea}Silence is a kindness you can always choose.{/idea}
old: I am only repeating what everyone is already saying.
new: Passing on a story about someone puts its weight on me too.
try: The next time a story about someone reaches you, do not forward it. Let it stop with you.

title: Known by their dignity, so they are not harassed.
subtitle: Covering as identity and protection

row.title: a sign of who I am

then: Allah told the Prophet ﷺ to tell his wives, daughters, and the believing women to draw their outer garments over themselves when going out. Ibn Kathir says this was so that {idea}they would be known and distinct{/idea} and not be harassed. The verse ends with {reward}Allah Forgiving and Merciful{/reward} for what came before.
now: What you wear says something before you speak, on the train, at the office, in the photo on your profile. {idea}Clothing can carry identity and dignity.{/idea} Whatever your own step, Allah meets it with forgiveness and mercy.
old: What I wear is only about style or comfort.
new: What I wear can carry who I am and what I value, before I say a word.
try: Before you go out today, ask yourself what your appearance says about what you value.

title: Those who spread alarm in the city were given a deadline.
subtitle: Stop spreading panic, or lose your place
then: In Madinah some people kept saying {trap}the enemy has come, war has started{/trap}, which Ibn Kathir calls a lie and a fabrication. Allah warned them that {idea}unless they gave this up and returned to the truth{/idea}, they would not remain neighbors in the city for long.
now: A voice note goes around: the bank is collapsing, the school is closing, something terrible is coming. You feel the urge to warn everyone. {trap}Panic travels faster than facts.{/trap} {idea}Checking before sharing protects your whole community.{/idea}
old: If I warn people about something scary, I am only being helpful.
new: Spreading alarm without checking can harm a whole community from inside.
try: Before you forward any alarming news today, check it with one reliable source.

title: Persisting in betrayal leaves no safe place.
subtitle: What happens when the warning is ignored
then: This verse continues the warning to the hypocrites and rumor spreaders of Madinah. Ibn Kathir says it describes their state if they {trap}persisted and did not give it up{/trap}: few, weak, and without shelter. {idea}The warning before it was a door to turn back through.{/idea}
now: You know a habit of yours is quietly damaging people around you, and you have been warned before. You tell yourself it will not catch up with you. {idea}Every warning is also an invitation to stop while the door is open.{/idea}
old: If I keep my wrongs hidden, they will never catch up with me.
new: A warning from Allah is a mercy, a chance to turn back before it is late.
try: Name one warning you have been ignoring. Take one step today to act on it.

title: Allah's way does not change.
subtitle: The same pattern across history

row.title: it will be different for me

then: Ibn Kathir explains that this is how Allah dealt with hypocrites who persisted in the past: {idea}the believers prevailed over them{/idea}. The verse adds that {trap}you will find no change in Allah's way{/trap}. What happened before follows the same law today.
now: You read about people who wrecked their lives through lies or greed, and you think: that would never happen to me. The same shortcuts are on your desk. {idea}Allah's ways are steady.{/idea} That is a warning, and also something you can build a life on.
old: The rules that caught others will not apply to me.
new: Allah's way does not change, so I can learn from those before me.
try: Think of one story of someone who fell. Name the first small step they took, and avoid it.

title: When is the Hour? Only Allah knows. It may be near.
subtitle: The right question is not when
then: People asked the Prophet ﷺ when the Hour would come. Allah told him to say that {idea}knowledge of it is with Allah alone{/idea}, and yet {trap}it may be near{/trap}. Ibn Kathir links this to verses saying the Hour and the reckoning have drawn close while people turn away.
now: Videos about the signs of the end get millions of views. People argue over dates and theories. {idea}The verse turns the question around: not when, but are you ready?{/idea}
old: If I knew when the end was coming, I would get serious.
new: Not knowing when is the point. I prepare now because it may be near.
try: Instead of reading about end-times signs today, do one thing you would want done before it.

title: Rejecting the truth means distance from His mercy.
subtitle: What the curse means
then: Right after the question about the Hour, Allah says He has cursed the disbelievers. Ibn Kathir explains the curse as {trap}being distanced from His mercy{/trap}, with a Fire prepared in the Hereafter. The passage is a sober warning about what turning away leads to.
now: You notice small moments where you push away reminders. You skip the talk, mute the friend who invites you to pray, scroll past the verse. {idea}Distance from mercy starts with small turns away.{/idea} Turning back starts the same way.
old: Ignoring reminders now and then does not really move me anywhere.
new: Each turn away moves me from mercy, and each turn back brings me near.
try: Accept one reminder today that you would normally scroll past or avoid.

title: There, no protector and no helper.
subtitle: When every connection runs out
then: The verse describes those who rejected the truth abiding in the Fire. Ibn Kathir explains that {trap}they will have no savior to help or rescue them{/trap}. Every person they relied on in this world will be gone.
now: In this world you have numbers to call: the cousin who knows someone, the lawyer, the friend with influence. {idea}There is a place where none of those numbers work.{/idea} The only connection that holds there is the one with Allah, built here.
old: I have people who can get me out of any trouble.
new: Only my connection with Allah holds where every other help runs out.
try: Before calling anyone about a problem today, make a short dua about it first.

title: If only we had obeyed Allah and the Messenger.
subtitle: A regret you can avoid today
then: On that Day, people in the Fire will say: {trap}if only we had obeyed Allah and obeyed the Messenger{/trap}. Ibn Kathir links it to the verse where the wrongdoer bites his hands, wishing he had taken a path with the Messenger. {idea}The wish is the same one available to anyone today.{/idea}
now: You picture yourself old, looking back. Which if onlys would you have? If only I had prayed more, called my mother, quit that job. {idea}Every if only you can name now is one you can still fix.{/idea}
old: I will get serious about obeying Allah later.
new: The regret of that Day can be avoided by what I choose today.
try: Write down one if only you would hate to have at the end. Do something about it today.

title: We just followed our leaders, they say.
subtitle: Following does not remove responsibility
then: In the Fire they will say: {trap}our Lord, we obeyed our chiefs and great ones, and they misled us{/trap}. Tawus said chiefs means their nobles and great ones means their scholars. {idea}Pointing to those they followed does not lift the burden.{/idea}
now: Your boss says cut the corner. Your favorite influencer says it is fine. Your friend group says everyone does it. {trap}Following is easy.{/trap} {idea}On that Day, you answer for who you chose to follow.{/idea}
old: If I follow someone respected, the responsibility is on them.
new: I answer for who I follow, so I check their path against Allah's.
try: Think of one person whose advice you follow without question. Check one of their views today.

title: Followers turn on their leaders when it is too late.
subtitle: Loyalty that ends in blame
then: The followers ask Allah to {trap}give their leaders double the punishment{/trap}, for their disbelief and for misleading others. Ibn Kathir reports that a man at a battle in the time of 'Ali recited these words to the Ansar, warning them {idea}not to become people who would one day say this{/idea}.
now: You see it at work: a team follows a manager into a mess, then everyone blames him when it falls apart. {trap}Blame comes after the damage is done.{/trap} {idea}The time to choose who you follow is before.{/idea}
old: If things go wrong, I can always blame those who led me.
new: Blaming leaders later fixes nothing. I choose carefully now.
try: Ask yourself where one of the people you follow is leading you. Be honest.

title: Do not be like those who hurt Musa with false talk.
subtitle: Allah cleared him of what they said
then: The Prophet ﷺ said Musa was {idea}a very shy and modest man{/idea}, and some of his people hurt him by claiming he covered himself because of some defect. Allah cleared him. When a man once accused the Prophet ﷺ of unfairness in sharing spoils, he said: {reward}may Allah have mercy on Musa, he was hurt with worse than this and was patient{/reward}.
now: A quiet colleague keeps to herself, and the office starts guessing why: she thinks she is better, she is hiding something. {trap}Modesty gets read as a secret.{/trap} {idea}Allah defends the modest.{/idea}
old: When someone keeps to themselves, there must be a reason worth guessing.
new: Guessing bad things about the modest hurts them. Allah clears them in the end.
try: Next time you start to guess why someone keeps private, stop and assume the best.

title: Fear Allah and say what is straight.
subtitle: Words with no twist in them
then: After warning against hurting the Prophet ﷺ as Musa was hurt with words, Allah commands the believers to have taqwa and speak {idea}qawlan sadida{/idea}. Ibn Kathir explains it as speaking in a straightforward way, {trap}with no crookedness or distortion{/trap}.
now: Your manager asks if the report is done. You say it is basically finished. It is not. Nobody lied exactly. {trap}The twist is in the word basically.{/trap} {idea}Straight speech leaves no gap between what you say and what is true.{/idea}
old: As long as I do not tell an outright lie, a little spin is fine.
new: Taqwa shows in my words. Straight speech has no twist hidden in it.
try: Catch one moment today where you would usually spin the truth. Say it straight instead.

title: Straight words, and Allah fixes your deeds.
subtitle: The promise for honest speech
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah promises those who fear Him and speak the truth that {reward}He will enable them to do righteous deeds and forgive their past sins{/reward}, and inspire them to repent from future ones. Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger ﷺ {idea}has achieved a great success{/idea}.
now: Your life feels like a pile of loose ends: habits you cannot fix, mistakes you cannot undo. You do not know where to start. {idea}The verse gives a starting point: fear Allah and speak straight.{/idea} He handles the mending.
old: I have to fix everything in my life before Allah will help me.
new: If I fear Allah and speak true, He sets my deeds right and forgives me.
try: Start with your words today. Speak straight in one hard conversation and leave the rest to Allah.

title: Mountains declined the trust that humans picked up.
subtitle: The weight of being responsible
then: Ibn 'Abbas said the trust means the duties: if fulfilled, rewarded; if neglected, punished. {idea}The heavens, earth, and mountains declined out of respect, fearing they could not fulfill it.{/idea} Man took it on, and the verse calls him unjust and ignorant, because he underestimated it. Ibn Kathir adds: {reward}except those whom Allah helps{/reward}.
now: Your prayer, your promises, your money, your children, your private moments. They feel like ordinary pieces of life. {idea}Each one is part of a trust the mountains were afraid to carry.{/idea} You do not carry it alone if you ask for help.
old: My daily duties are just the routine parts of life.
new: My duties are a trust the mountains refused. I carry it by asking Allah's help.
try: Pick one duty you treat lightly. Do it today as if you were carrying something precious.

title: The trust sorts people, and mercy waits for believers.
subtitle: The last word of Al-Ahzab
then: Because humans took on the trust, Ibn Kathir explains, people are sorted by how they bore it. {trap}The hypocrites and those who associate partners with Allah{/trap} face punishment. {reward}Allah turns in mercy to the believing men and women.{/reward} The surah ends with Allah Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.
now: You read about the trust and feel the weight of everything you have failed to carry well. The last line of the surah is for you: {reward}Allah turns to the believers{/reward}. {idea}The trust is heavy, and the forgiveness is wide.{/idea}
old: I have dropped the trust too many times for it to count.
new: Allah turns in mercy to believers who keep trying. His forgiveness is wide.
